Born from a love of the back roads

Rond-Point was born from a love of the back roads and a desire to do road trips better. France has more roundabouts than anywhere on Earth, and we came to think of every one of them as an invitation: go straight on to the motorway, or take the third exit towards a village you've never heard of.

We kept taking the third exit. It led to lunches that lasted until four, to a château owner who insisted we stay for the harvest, to a lavender field nobody had photographed. The long way round turned out to be the whole point.

So we built a company around it. Every Rond-Point trip is a loop: you set off, take the long way round through vineyards, villages, coastlines and mountain passes, and come back to where you started, changed. Real local knowledge goes into every kilometre, and one specialist stays with you the whole way.

In winter, the black Périgord truffle comes to market in Sarlat, Sainte-Alvère and nearby towns. Buyers sniff, sellers shrug, prices are whispered. Go for the theatre, stay for the omelette.
Burgundy's winegrowers honour their patron saint in a different village each year (hence 'tournante': it goes round, like us). Processions, paper flowers and a great deal of tasting.
The high passes close and the Alps turn into ski country. A winter loop swaps cols for chalets, fondue and a car with winter tyres or chains.
The hills between Bormes-les-Mimosas and Grasse turn bright yellow and smell of honey. The Route du Mimosa links the villages; the sunshine is free.
Menton's Fête du Citron builds giant sculptures from tonnes of lemons and oranges, with parades along the seafront. Very yellow, extremely zesty.
Two weeks of floats, giant heads and flower battles, where costumed performers throw blooms into the crowd along the Promenade des Anglais.
Before the lavender, the orchards: almond, cherry and apricot trees flower across the Luberon and the Comtat Venaissin, with snow still on Ventoux.
Tulips, wisteria and freshly clipped box hedges: the Loire's château gardens, from Villandry to Chenonceau, look their best in spring, before the summer crowds.
Apple blossom in the Pays d'Auge
Orchards full of pink and white blossom between half-timbered farmhouses. Some villages hold blossom festivals; cider producers open their doors.
Napoleon said he could smell Corsica from the sea. In spring, cistus, myrtle and broom flower across the maquis, the roads are quiet and the sea is just about swimmable.
Thousands of sheep, goats and donkeys parade through Saint-Rémy-de-Provence before heading up to the summer pastures. Get there early and stand well back.
Ceremonies, parachute drops and parades of restored vehicles mark the anniversary of the landings along the Normandy beaches. Moving and very busy; book well ahead.
On the longest day, all of France turns into a free concert. Strasbourg and Colmar fill with bands on every corner; a wine-village square with an accordion is just as good.
Snowploughs clear the Iseran, the Galibier and the Bonette, often between walls of snow. Opening dates depend on the winter, so we check before every trip.
The plateaux of Valensole and Sault turn purple, with Valensole often peaking in early July and Sault a little later. Harvest starts in mid-July, so don't leave it too late.
Fields of sunflowers turn to face the morning sun across the Périgord and Provence. Pull over, safely, and join everyone else taking the same photo.
One of the world's great theatre festivals takes over Avignon, from the Palais des Papes courtyard to hundreds of fringe shows in every cellar and chapel.
France's national day brings fireworks everywhere, but Carcassonne's display over its medieval walls is legendary. The whole Cité appears to be on fire. It isn't.
Bayonne dresses in white and red for five days of music, dancing and Basque traditions. It's joyful, crowded and loud, so plan to stay outside town.
Ten days of pipes, fiddles, dance and Celtic culture from Brittany, Scotland, Ireland, Galicia and beyond. The grand parade is a sight (and sound) to behold.
The Perseid meteor shower peaks in mid-August. From a high valley far from city lights, lie back on a warm rock and count. Some villages switch off their streetlights for it.
Pickers fill the slopes, tractors fill the lanes and the whole Côte smells of crushed grapes. Some estates pause visits during harvest, so we book around it.
Every grape in Champagne is picked by hand, so the harvest is a busy, joyful affair with presses running day and night in every village.
From Saint-Émilion to the Médoc, the vendanges roll from white grapes to red through September and into October. Golden light, busy cellars.
As the crowds leave, the Atlantic swells arrive. Warm water, bigger waves and empty beaches: the surfers' favourite season.
Walnut trees and oak woods turn gold, mist hangs over the river in the mornings and the cèpe hunters are out. The castles look even better in it.
After the harvest, the Alsace vineyards turn gold and red, and winstubs serve 'vin nouveau' (barely fermented new wine) with walnuts and onion tart.
In the Castagniccia and around the island's mountain villages, chestnuts are gathered for flour, cakes and polenta. Village fairs celebrate the harvest into early winter.
The first wine of the vintage is released at midnight, and bars from Beaujeu to Beaune celebrate. It's young, fruity and not to be taken too seriously, which is exactly the point.
Strasbourg, Colmar, Kaysersberg and Riquewihr light up with wooden chalets, mulled wine and bredele biscuits. The most festive road trip in Europe; book early.
Reims hosts a big Christmas market beside its cathedral, and the cellars are in a festive mood. The perfect time to stock up for New Year's Eve.

Keep right, overtake on the left, and take extra care at the first junction of the day.
France drives on the right and overtakes on the left. Undertaking (passing on the right) is not allowed on motorways, except in slow-moving queues where lanes move at different speeds.

If you're used to driving on the left, the riskiest moments are the quiet ones: pulling out of a car park, turning left at an empty junction or setting off after lunch. A little 'keep right' note on the dashboard is not embarrassing; it's clever.

On a single-carriageway road, the driver should sit nearest the centre line. In a right-hand-drive car, overtaking is harder to judge, so give yourself more room and let your passenger be a second pair of eyes.
Traffic already on the roundabout usually has priority. Go anticlockwise and signal right before your exit.

France has more roundabouts than any other country in the world, so you'll get plenty of practice. You go round anticlockwise, and on most roundabouts you give way to traffic already circulating (coming from your left). They're marked with a give-way triangle and the sign 'Vous n'avez pas la priorité' (you do not have priority).

A few older roundabouts and squares, most famously Place Charles-de-Gaulle around the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, have no give-way signs. There, the general priorité à droite rule applies, so traffic entering from the right has priority over traffic already on the roundabout. Approach any roundabout without give-way markings with care.

Use the right lane if you're taking the first or second exit, and an inner lane for later exits, moving back to the outside before your exit. Always signal right just before you leave. And if you miss your exit? Go round again. It's practically our motto.
At unmarked junctions, traffic coming from your right has priority, even from a tiny side road.

France's famous 'priorité à droite' means that, unless signs or road markings say otherwise, vehicles joining from the right have priority. It still applies at many junctions in towns, villages and the countryside, and it catches visitors out.

On main roads, a yellow diamond sign means you have priority over side roads; the same sign with a black line through it means that priority has ended, so watch for cars from the right. A red-bordered triangle with a black cross warns that priority to the right applies at the next junction.
In practice: slow down at junctions in villages, look right, and don't be surprised if a small Renault pulls out without hesitation. Legally, it was its turn.

Default limits for cars are: 130 km/h on motorways (110 km/h in rain); 110 km/h on dual carriageways separated by a central reservation (100 km/h in rain); 80 km/h on two-way roads without a central separation, though some departments have restored 90 km/h on certain roads, so follow the signs; and 50 km/h in built-up areas, which start at the town's name sign.
Many cities, including Paris, Lyon and Grenoble, have set 30 km/h limits on most streets. In fog or other poor visibility (under 50 metres), the limit is 50 km/h everywhere.

Drivers with a probationary licence (newly qualified) have lower limits: 110 km/h on motorways, 100 on dual carriageways and 80 on other roads. Check how this applies to you if you have recently passed your test.
Speed cameras are common and often unmarked. Fines for foreign-registered and rental cars are pursued across borders, and your rental company will pass them on with an admin fee.
Most motorways charge tolls, paid by card at the booth, by tag, or online on newer barrier-free sections.

Most French motorways (autoroutes) are toll roads, shown by the word 'péage'. On most, you take a ticket on entry and pay at a barrier on exit; others charge a fixed amount at a toll plaza. Bank cards, including contactless, are widely accepted. Avoid lanes marked only with an orange 't', which are for electronic tags.
A télépéage tag (badge) lets you drive through dedicated lanes and pay by monthly bill. It's handy if you'll use a lot of motorways; on most of our loops, you won't.

Some newer sections use barrier-free 'free-flow' tolling: cameras read your number plate and you pay online within a set deadline (usually a few days). If you don't pay, a fine follows, so we flag these sections in your route book.
Toll prices rise every year. As a rough guide, Paris to Lyon costs several tens of euros for a car. Check routes and costs with the motorway operators before you go.
Check the pump label (gazole is diesel) and plan EV charging stops on rural and mountain days.

Fuel names to know: 'gazole' is diesel (B7, sometimes B10 or XTL), 'SP95' and 'SP98' are unleaded petrol (E5), and 'SP95-E10' is unleaded with up to 10% ethanol, fine for most modern petrol cars. 'E85' is high-ethanol fuel for compatible cars only. Check the label inside your rental car's fuel flap.
Supermarket fuel stations are usually cheapest, motorway stations the most expensive. Many rural stations are automated at night and on Sundays, accepting only chip-and-PIN bank cards.

Electric cars: fast chargers are found at most motorway service areas, and slower chargers in towns, supermarkets and many hotels. Coverage is thinner in the mountains and deep countryside, so plan stops ahead with a charging app and carry a card or app that works across several networks.
Pay-and-display or apps in towns; a parking disc in blue zones; never park on yellow lines.

In most towns, on-street parking is paid at a machine (horodateur), often by card or through a parking app, and you may need to enter your number plate. Charges usually apply on weekdays and Saturdays, with free parking at lunchtime in some smaller towns; check the machine.

Blue zones (zone bleue) offer free short-term parking with a parking disc (disque de stationnement) on the dashboard showing your arrival time. Rental cars usually have one; if not, they're sold cheaply at tobacconists and petrol stations.
Yellow lines on the kerb mean no parking. In popular villages, use the car parks at the edge of town; the walk in is part of the experience, and the lanes weren't built for cars anyway.
Some cities restrict polluting vehicles using Crit'Air stickers. Rules are in flux: check before you go.

Several French cities and metropolitan areas have operated low-emission zones (zones à faibles émissions, ZFE), where vehicles must display a Crit'Air sticker showing their emissions class. Stickers are also used for temporary restrictions during pollution peaks.

The national framework for ZFEs has been under review, with lawmakers voting in 2025 to scrap or scale back the scheme. The situation in each city may differ, so check the current rules before you drive into a big city.

Rental cars registered in France usually already have a sticker. If you bring your own car, buy a Crit'Air sticker only from the official site, certificat-air.gouv.fr, which costs a few euros. Unofficial sites charge far more for the same sticker.
Carry your licence, passport or ID, the rental agreement or registration document, and proof of insurance.

Always carry: your full, valid driving licence; your passport or national ID card; the car's registration document (for a rental, the rental agreement does the job); and proof of insurance. Police can ask to see them at any time.

Licences issued in the EU and EEA are valid in France. Many other licences are accepted for short visits, but some must be accompanied by an International Driving Permit (IDP) or an official French translation, and some rental partners ask for an IDP regardless. Check the rules for your licence country with official sources and with us.
If you bring a UK-registered car, display a 'UK' identifier (sticker or on the number plate) and carry your V5C registration certificate and insurance documents.
A hi-vis vest within reach and a warning triangle are compulsory; headlamp adjustments for right-hand-drive cars.

Every car must carry a high-visibility vest, kept within reach of the driver (not in the boot), and a warning triangle. If you break down, put the vest on before you get out. Rental cars should come equipped; check before you drive off.

French law has required drivers to carry a breathalyser since 2012, but the fine for not having one was dropped, so in practice no penalty applies. A disposable one in the glovebox is still a good idea. Spare bulbs are recommended rather than compulsory.

If you bring a right-hand-drive car, adjust or fit beam deflectors so your headlights don't dazzle oncoming drivers. In mountain areas, some winter rules require snow tyres or chains between 1 November and 31 March; they don't apply to our summer Alpine loops but do to winter trips.
Shop a Luberon market with a local cook, then turn the haul into lunch in a farmhouse kitchen. You'll leave knowing how to pick a melon by its weight and a tomato by its smell.
Walk the rows with a family of lavender growers on the Valensole plateau, then watch the copper stills turn a field into a few precious drops. Best in late June and July.
Paddle from the Lac de Sainte-Croix into the mouth of the gorge, between limestone walls and water the colour of a boiled sweet. No experience needed, just sun cream.
In the hill town that taught the world to smell nice, a perfumer helps you blend your own eau de toilette. Name it after your favourite hairpin.
Meet the herders and the cows behind the great Alpine cheeses at a summer dairy below the passes, then taste wheels of different ages. The cows are unimpressed by your car.
E-bike to Chenonceau on the Loire à Vélo
Follow quiet lanes and riverside paths from Amboise to the château that spans the Cher, with a picnic stop and a tasting on the way back. Pedal-assist does the hills; you do the photos.
Descend into cellars carved into the soft tufa cliffs and taste Chinon and Saumur reds with a family winegrower. It's a steady 12°C down there; bring a jumper, even in July.
Ride the Voie des Vignes through Pommard, Volnay and Meursault, past walls that separate some of the most valuable vineyards on earth. Lunch in a village square, tasting in a cellar.
A small domaine, a cellar that smells of oak and damp stone, and a winemaker who will happily explain climats until the sun goes down. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, straight from the barrel.
Riesling to Gewurztraminer with a winegrower
Taste your way across the Alsace grape varieties with a family winegrower in a village cellar, from bone-dry Riesling to honeyed late harvests. Kugelhopf may appear.

Follow a truffle farmer and a very focused dog through the oak trees, then taste the black diamonds on toast with a glass of something local. Summer truffles from May, black Périgord truffles in winter.
Drift down the Dordogne past Castelnaud, Beynac and La Roque-Gageac, with a pebble beach for lunch. A minibus brings you back to the start. The river does most of the work.

Timed tickets for the Vézère valley's painted caves and their faithful replicas, where bison and horses have been galloping across the walls for some 20,000 years. We handle the booking; you handle the goosebumps.
A local guide rides along in your car from Arromanches to Omaha, Pointe du Hoc and Utah Beach, telling the stories behind the monuments. Moving, precise and never rushed.
Barefoot across the bay to Mont-Saint-Michel
Cross the sands to the Mont with a qualified bay guide, timed to the tides. Quicksand, crossing channels and the best view of the abbey there is. Never attempt it without a guide.
Oysters at low tide in Cancale
Walk out to the oyster beds with a producer, learn the difference between a creuse and a plate, then eat them on the harbour wall with lemon and bread. Bring an appetite, leave the shells.
A traditional sailing boat, a skipper who knows every current, and islands for picnicking. The gulf's tides race through the narrows; let someone local take the helm.
Cliff-top lanes from Saint-Jean-de-Luz to Hendaye, with the Pyrenees dropping into the Atlantic and Spain waving from across the bay. Stop for a swim, a coffee and another swim.
Surf lesson on the Basque coast
A friendly instructor, a soft board and a beach with forgiving waves. Standing up is likely; looking cool doing it is a work in progress.
From Porto, a small boat slips past the red cliffs of the Scandola nature reserve to the fishing hamlet of Girolata, reachable only by sea or on foot. Ospreys overhead, if you're lucky.
Chestnut-fed charcuterie, brocciu cheese and a glass of island wine at a farm in the hills, with the family who made all of it. Lunch tends to end around tea time.
Descend into chalk cellars where millions of bottles rest in the dark, learn why they're turned by hand, then taste a range from blanc de blancs to rosé. A grower or a grande maison, your choice.
Pedal-assisted lanes from Hautvillers along the slopes of the Marne valley, with a picnic among the vines and a grower's tasting at the end. Every hill is easier with bubbles at the top.
A family château outside the medieval village, a walk through Merlot vines on the limestone plateau and a tasting of several vintages. Then the village itself, one steep cobbled street at a time.
What's included in a Rond-Point road trip?

Every loop includes hand-picked stays (boutique hotels, châteaux, farmhouses and the odd fisherman's house), car hire with a full-insurance option, a beautifully printed route book plus an offline app version, and one dedicated specialist on WhatsApp seven days a week for the whole trip.

We also book the things that need booking (restaurant tables, cave tickets, tastings, e-bikes and guides) and send you local tips you won't find in a guidebook. Each trip page lists exactly what's included and what isn't.
Not included: flights or trains to France, fuel, tolls, parking, most meals and personal travel insurance. We're happy to advise on any of them.
How does the WhatsApp specialist support work?

The same person who designed your trip stays with you while you're on the road. Message them on WhatsApp for anything: a dinner recommendation, a change of plan, a flat tyre, a sudden craving for oysters.
Your specialist is available seven days a week during your trip, from [8:00 to 20:00] Paris time, with an emergency line outside those hours. Replies are usually within minutes, not hours.
When is the best time to go?
It depends on the corner of France. Late spring (May–June) and early autumn (September–October) are lovely almost everywhere: warm, green or golden, and quieter than high summer.

Some highlights are seasonal. Provence's lavender usually flowers from late June to mid-July, the high Alpine passes are generally open from about June to October, the grape harvest runs roughly from late August to early October, and Alsace's Christmas markets fill late November and December. Our When to go calendar has the details, and dates shift year to year, so we always check before we plan.
How does car hire and insurance work?

We arrange your car with a reputable rental partner, collected at the airport or station where your loop begins and ends. Standard hire includes the legally required third-party cover; we strongly recommend the full-insurance option, which reduces your excess (deductible) to [zero or a small amount].

You'll need a credit card in the main driver's name for the rental deposit. Additional drivers can be added at the counter. We'll send you a checklist before you travel so the pick-up takes minutes, not an hour.
Verify before launch: confirm the rental partner's insurance terms, excess amounts and deposit rules.
Do I need an International Driving Permit?

It depends on where your licence was issued. Licences from EU and EEA countries are valid in France. A UK photocard licence is generally accepted for visits without an International Driving Permit (IDP), though an older paper licence may need one.

Licences from many other countries (including the USA, Canada and Australia) are usually accepted for short visits, but some must be accompanied by an IDP or an official translation, and some rental partners ask for an IDP regardless. Check with us and with official sources for your country before you travel; an IDP is inexpensive and can save an awkward conversation at the rental desk.
Verify before launch: rules depend on licence country and can change.
Can I have an automatic car?

Yes, but you need to ask. Manual gearboxes are still the default for hire cars in France, so automatics are in shorter supply and cost more. Tell us when you enquire and we'll guarantee an automatic in your booking.
If you usually drive an automatic, we'd recommend one: hill starts in a medieval village with a tractor behind you are not the moment to rediscover the clutch.

Not on our trips. Every Rond-Point road trip is a loop that starts and ends at the same airport or station, which is the main reason we design them that way: one-way fees within France can be steep, and dropping a car in another country can cost several hundred euros.
If you'd like to end somewhere else, we can quote it, and we'll always show you the fee upfront.
Can I do my road trip in an electric car?
Yes. France has a large and growing charging network, with fast chargers at most motorway service areas and plenty of slower chargers in towns, supermarket car parks and at many hotels.

We plan EV loops with realistic daily distances, note charging points in your route book and choose stays with charging where possible. Rural and mountain areas have fewer fast chargers, so we build in a charging stop rather than hoping for one. A charging app or aggregator (Chargemap is a popular one) and a card or app that works on several networks make life easier.
Verify before launch: confirm EV availability with the rental partner for each pick-up location.
How do French motorway tolls work?

Most French motorways (autoroutes) are toll roads, marked 'péage'. You take a ticket on entry and pay on exit, or pay a fixed amount at a barrier. Bank cards, including contactless, are accepted at almost all booths; use the lanes marked with a card symbol and avoid the 't' (télépéage) lanes unless you have a tag.

Some newer sections use barrier-free 'free-flow' tolling, where cameras read your number plate and you pay online within a set time. We flag these in your route book. As a rough guide, a long motorway day can cost €20–40 in tolls, but our loops spend most of their time on toll-free D-roads, which is where the good stuff is anyway.
Verify before launch: toll prices and free-flow sections change regularly.
What are low-emission zones and Crit'Air stickers?

Several French cities have operated low-emission zones (zones à faibles émissions, ZFE) where vehicles need a Crit'Air sticker showing their emissions class, and stickers can also be required during pollution-peak restrictions. The rules have been under review at national level, so the situation in each city can change.

Rental cars registered in France usually already carry a Crit'Air sticker, but check when you collect the car. If you're bringing your own car, order a sticker only from the official site, certificat-air.gouv.fr. Copycat sites charge much more for the same thing.
Verify before launch: ZFE rules are changing; confirm the current status city by city.
How fit do I need to be for the e-bike days?

If you can ride a bike, you can do our e-bike days. Pedal-assist e-bikes boost your effort up to 25 km/h (the legal limit for e-bikes in Europe), so hills feel like gentle slopes and headwinds become a rumour.

Rides are typically 25–45 km with plenty of stops, mostly on quiet lanes and cycle paths. We deliver the bikes to your stay, fitted and charged, with helmets, locks, panniers and a route on a handlebar-mounted phone holder. If the weather turns, your specialist will help you swap the ride for a drive.
Can we travel with children? What about car seats?

Absolutely: road trips are brilliant with children, and we plan shorter driving days, family rooms and plenty of things to climb. Tell us your children's ages, heights and weights and we'll book the right seats with the car.

In France, children generally must use a child restraint suited to their size until they are 10 years old, and EU rules require a restraint for children under 135 cm. Children under 10 may not normally sit in the front seat, with limited exceptions (for example a rear-facing baby seat with the front airbag deactivated). Verify before launch: confirm the current rules with official sources.
What is the EU Entry/Exit System (EES)?

The Entry/Exit System is the EU's digital border system for non-EU travellers on short stays in the Schengen area, including France. It replaces passport stamps: on your first entry, your fingerprints and a photo are taken at the border, along with your passport details.

It's in operation now, so allow a little extra time at your first border crossing, especially at busy airports and the Channel ports. Later visits should be quicker. EU citizens and residents aren't affected.
Verify before launch: check the official EU travel pages for the latest guidance.
Will I need ETIAS to visit France?

Coming soon: ETIAS (the European Travel Information and Authorisation System) will require visa-exempt visitors, such as travellers from the UK, USA, Canada and Australia, to apply online for a travel authorisation before visiting France and most of Europe. The fee is expected to be €20.

Its launch has been postponed to 2027 and there is no firm date yet. You don't need it today, and we'll update this page (and let you know before you travel) as soon as it goes live. Only apply through the official EU website when it opens.

The best road trips in France
Lavender plateaux, Alpine passes, castle-lined rivers and island hairpins: our pick of France's greatest drives, and how to do them properly.

France is the most rewarding road-trip country in Europe, and it isn't close. It has the space (it's the biggest country in the EU), the variety (Alps, Atlantic, Mediterranean, and everything in between) and the roads: around a million kilometres of them, most of them small, quiet and leading somewhere that serves lunch.

The trick is to stay off the motorways. The autoroutes are fast and efficient, but the real France lives on the D-roads, the departmental roads that wander from village to village, through vineyards and over passes. Every loop below is designed around them. And every one is a loop, so you finish where you started without paying a one-way fee.

The classic, and for good reason. From Marseille, head into the Luberon, where Gordes, Roussillon and Bonnieux sit on their hilltops like they're waiting for a painter. Then cross the lavender plateaux of Sault and Valensole, drop into the Verdon gorges and finish on the coast at Cassis.

Timing matters. The lavender usually flowers from late June to mid-July, with the Valensole plateau often at its best in early July. Come in May or September instead and you'll trade purple fields for empty villages and long, warm evenings. Neither is a bad deal.

If you love driving, this is the one. The Route des Grandes Alpes runs from Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean over the most famous passes in Europe: the Col de l'Iseran, the highest paved pass in the Alps at 2,764 m, plus the Galibier, the Izoard and the Bonette.

Our version starts on the Riviera, climbs through the red gorges of the Cians and spends a week among the cols before dropping back to the sea. The passes are generally open from around June to October, depending on snow.
3. The Dordogne: castles, caves and canoes

The Dordogne valley is road-trip perfection in miniature. Distances are short, the roads are gentle and there's a castle on every other cliff: Beynac, Castelnaud, Montfort. Add the painted caves of the Vézère valley, the cliff town of Rocamadour, a canoe trip and the Saturday market in Sarlat, and you have a week that suits everyone from history buffs to small children.

It's also one of France's great food regions. Walnuts, duck, strawberries in spring, cèpes in autumn and black truffles in winter. Finish your loop in Saint-Émilion and you'll have covered the wine, too.
4. Normandy: the D-Day beaches and Mont-Saint-Michel

Some road trips are about scenery; this one is also about stories. From Honfleur's painterly harbour, drive through the cider country of the Pays d'Auge to Bayeux, then spend a day on the D-Day landing beaches with a local historian. It's the most moving day you'll spend in France.

Then head west to Mont-Saint-Michel. Stay nearby so you can see it at sunrise, and cross the bay on foot with a qualified guide: the tides here are among the strongest in Europe and the sands are not to be explored alone.

Corsica is a mountain range rising out of the sea, which means every road is either climbing, descending or hugging a cliff. The Calanches de Piana, the Col de Bavella and the coast road to Calvi are among the most spectacular drives anywhere in Europe.

Corsican roads are slow. A 100 km day can easily take three hours of driving. Plan fewer kilometres than you think, book an automatic if you're more comfortable with one, and expect to reverse for a coach at least once.
6. The gentle ones: Loire, Burgundy, Alsace

Not every road trip needs hairpins. The Loire Valley, Burgundy and Alsace are perfect for a slower pace, with short drives between châteaux, wine villages and some of the best food in France. They're also ideal for mixing driving with e-bike days: park the car outside your hotel and pedal the vineyard lanes instead.
The Loire: Renaissance châteaux, riverside cycle paths and wine cellars dug into the rock.
Burgundy: the Route des Grands Crus and the Voie des Vignes cycle path, with Beaune as your base.
Alsace: the Route des Vins through storybook villages, and the best Christmas markets in France.
7. Brittany and the Basque Country: the Atlantic edge

France's Atlantic coast is wilder and greener than the Mediterranean. Brittany has pink granite, lighthouses and crêperies; the Basque Country has surf, red-shuttered villages and the Pyrenees as a backdrop. Both are at their best from June to September, and both are seriously good places to eat.
A few things we've learned on the road
Plan fewer kilometres than you think. France is big, the small roads are slow and the best moments happen when you stop.
Lunch is the main event. In rural France, kitchens often close by 2pm, so aim to be at the table by 1pm.
Book an automatic if you need one. Manual is still the default for hire cars, and automatics run out in summer.
Avoid driving into big cities. Park outside and take a tram, or skip them on a road trip altogether.
Fill up at supermarkets. Motorway fuel is the most expensive, and rural stations may only take chip-and-PIN cards at night.

Start with the season. Spring is for gardens, blossom and the Loire. Early summer is for lavender and the Alps. Autumn is for harvests, golden vineyards and the Dordogne. Winter is for truffles, Christmas markets and the Riviera's mimosa. Our When to go calendar has the details, month by month.

Then think about pace. Do you want long, glorious days at the wheel, or short hops and long lunches? We grade every trip Gentle, Balanced or Ambitious, so you know what you're getting into. And if you can't decide, tell us what you love and let us take the long way round for you.

How to drive a French roundabout like a local
France has more roundabouts than any country on earth. Here's how to tackle them with confidence, from give-way rules to the Arc de Triomphe.

We named our company after them, so we'd better explain. France has tens of thousands of roundabouts (ronds-points), more than any other country in the world. Small towns have them at both ends; some villages seem to have more roundabouts than residents. Many are decorated by the local council with sculptures, flower beds, vintage tractors or, in one memorable case we know, a giant snail.

For visitors, especially those used to driving on the left, roundabouts are often the most nerve-racking part of driving in France. They needn't be. Here's how to handle them like a local, minus the hand gestures.
The golden rule: give way to traffic already on the roundabout

On the vast majority of French roundabouts, traffic already circulating has priority, and you give way before entering. You'll see a red-bordered give-way triangle (cédez le passage), dashed give-way lines on the road and, usually, a sign saying 'Vous n'avez pas la priorité': you do not have priority.

Because France drives on the right, you go round anticlockwise, and the traffic you're giving way to is coming from your left. If you're used to driving on the left, that's the mirror image of what you know, and the moment to slow down and think.
Remember: look left, give way to the left, go round to the right. If in doubt, stop and wait for a clear gap. Nobody minds a cautious driver; plenty of people mind a confused one.
Priorité à droite, the old way

Before the 1980s, French roundabouts followed the general rule of priorité à droite: traffic coming from the right had priority, which on a roundabout means cars entering have priority over cars already going round. Most roundabouts were converted to the modern give-way system, but not all.

The most famous exception is the Place Charles-de-Gaulle around the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, where twelve avenues feed a huge cobbled circle with no lanes and no give-way lines. Traffic entering from the right has priority. It works, in a very Parisian way, but we'd suggest admiring it from the pavement.

In smaller towns, you may still meet a roundabout with no give-way signs or markings. Treat it with caution: entering traffic from your right may have priority. Slow down, watch what others do and be ready to stop.
Many French roundabouts have a single lane, which makes life easy. On larger ones with two or more lanes, the general practice is straightforward:
For the first exit (turning right), approach in the right-hand lane, stay in it and signal right as you approach.
For exits straight ahead, the right-hand lane is usually fine; follow any lane markings or overhead signs.
For later exits, you can use the inner (left-hand) lane, then move carefully back to the outer lane before your exit, checking your mirror and blind spot.
Always signal right just before you leave the roundabout, after passing the exit before yours.
Watch for cyclists and motorbikes, who often stay on the outside of the roundabout.

Be aware that French drivers don't always signal on roundabouts, and some use the outer lane for every exit. Leave space, watch the wheels of the car next to you rather than its indicators, and don't assume anyone is leaving until they actually do.

Before each roundabout, a blue or green sign shows the layout and exits. Green signs point towards major roads and towns; blue ones towards motorways; white for local destinations. 'Toutes directions' (all directions) and 'Autres directions' (other directions) are your friends when your town isn't listed. Your route book uses exit numbers, just like our homepage.
Approaching, entering, and the people on foot

Slow down early: many roundabouts on the edge of towns come straight after a fast stretch of road, and the speed limit usually drops to 50 km/h or less on the approach. Pick your lane in good time, look left as you near the give-way line and judge the gap by the traffic, not by hope.

Zebra crossings often sit just before the entry and just after each exit. Pedestrians have priority when they're crossing or clearly about to cross, so leaving a roundabout means checking the crossing as well as your mirror. On mini-roundabouts in villages (a painted circle or a low dome), give way in the same way and go round the marking, not over it, if your car fits.
Large lorries and caravans need the whole width of the roundabout and may straddle both lanes. Hang back, let them through and don't try to squeeze alongside.
The most important rule of all

If you miss your exit, don't brake, don't swerve and don't reverse. Just go round again. A roundabout is the only road in the world that gives you a second chance by design, and the scenic route is rarely a mistake.

That's more or less our philosophy. Every Rond-Point trip is a loop: you start and finish in the same place, but the way round is the whole point. You'll probably meet a few hundred roundabouts on the way. By the end of the week, you'll be choosing your exit with a confident flick of the indicator and a nod to the giant snail.
A few more tips for driving in France
Priorité à droite also applies at many unmarked junctions in towns and villages: give way to traffic joining from the right unless signs tell you otherwise.
Speed limits drop sharply at the town sign, typically to 50 km/h, and often 30 km/h in city centres.
Keep a hi-vis vest within reach of the driver's seat and a warning triangle in the car.
In the countryside, tractors have every right to be there. Breathe, enjoy the view, overtake only when it's clearly safe.
Rules change. Check our Driving in France guide and the official French road safety website before you travel. Your specialist is on WhatsApp for any question, roundabout-related or otherwise.

Self-drive vs drive & e-bike: which loop is yours?
Four wheels or four wheels plus two? How our two styles of road trip compare, and how to choose the right one for you.

Every Rond-Point trip is a loop by car, with hand-picked stays, a route book and a specialist on WhatsApp. But we design two kinds: classic self-drive road trips, and 'drive & e-bike' trips, where some days you leave the car at the hotel and explore on a pedal-assisted bike instead. Here's how they compare.

A self-drive loop is the purest form of road trip. Every day brings a new stretch of road, from short hops between villages to big days over mountain passes. You cover more ground, see more landscapes and enjoy the drive as part of the experience.

Self-drive suits you if you love driving (or being driven), want to see a lot in a week, or are heading somewhere where distances are bigger and the roads are the highlight: the Alps, Corsica, the Verdon, the coast of Brittany.
Best for: drivers, dramatic scenery, covering a wider area, mountain passes.
Typical pace: Balanced or Ambitious, two to four hours at the wheel on most days.
Our favourites: the Riviera and Alpine passes, the Corsica island loop, the Brittany coast.
Drive & e-bike: the best of both

On a drive & e-bike trip, you still have a car for the whole loop, but on two to four days you'll swap it for an e-bike. Bikes are delivered to your stay, fitted, charged and ready, with helmets, locks, panniers and a route loaded on a handlebar phone mount.
Rides are typically 25–45 km, on cycle paths and quiet lanes, with stops for lunch, tastings and photographs. Then you're back at your hotel, and the car is ready for the next day's drive.

Why bother? Because some places are simply better by bike. You can't stop a car in the middle of a grand cru vineyard, but you can lean a bike against the wall. You can ride straight up to the gates of Chenonceau on a riverside path while everyone else hunts for parking. And you can taste wine at lunch without worrying about who's driving.

You don't need to be. Our e-bikes are pedal-assisted: a motor adds power as you pedal, up to 25 km/h (the legal limit for e-bikes in Europe). Hills feel like gentle slopes, and headwinds lose their bite. If you can ride a bike, you can do our e-bike days, and many guests who haven't ridden for years tell us it was the highlight of their trip.
Weather looking grim? Your specialist can swap an e-bike day for a drive at short notice. Nothing is fixed, and nobody gets wet who doesn't want to.
The Loire Valley: flat riverside paths on the Loire à Vélo route, with châteaux at every turn.
Burgundy: the Voie des Vignes cycle path through Pommard, Volnay and Meursault.
Champagne: vineyard lanes from Hautvillers along the Marne valley.
The Basque Country: cliff-top lanes along the Corniche and rolling hills inland.
Ask yourself three questions. First, how do you like to spend your days? If the drive itself is what excites you, go self-drive. If you prefer to slow right down and feel the landscape, add e-bikes.
Second, where are you going? Wine regions and river valleys are perfect for e-bikes; mountains and islands are better suited to the car (unless you're a very keen cyclist, in which case talk to us).

Third, who's coming? E-bike days are brilliant for couples and friends, and work well with teenagers. With younger children, a self-drive loop with shorter driving days and plenty of stops is usually easier, though we can add child seats or trailers to bikes in some regions.
What a typical day looks like

On a self-drive day, you might leave after breakfast, drive an hour and a half to a market town, wander and lunch, then take a scenic road to your next hotel, arriving in time for a swim before dinner. On a big day in the mountains, you'll spend longer at the wheel, with stops at belvederes and a picnic at the top of a pass.

On an e-bike day, there's no packing and no driving. The bikes are waiting when you come down to breakfast. You set off mid-morning, ride for an hour or two, stop for a tasting or a château, have lunch in a village square, then pedal gently home for a late-afternoon rest. Most guests ride between three and four hours in total, spread across the day.
Luggage stays at the hotel on e-bike days; carry only what you need in the panniers.
Helmets are provided and strongly recommended. They're compulsory in France for children under 12.
E-bike batteries last comfortably for our routes; we plan rides well within their range.
Our drive & e-bike loops are usually Gentle or Balanced, with shorter drives on the non-cycling days.
Prices include bike delivery, fitting, equipment and route navigation.

All our trips are tailor-made, so the line between the two styles is yours to draw. Add an e-bike day to a self-drive loop, or drop one from a drive & e-bike trip. Add a cooking class, a boat trip, an extra night where you fall in love with the view. Tell your specialist what you enjoy and the loop will bend around you. That's rather the point of a roundabout.

The best wine routes in France
From Alsace's flower-boxed villages to the grands crus of Burgundy and the chalk cellars of Champagne: France's great wine roads, and how to drive them.

France has some of the most beautiful wine country in the world, and the best way to see it is slowly, along the routes des vins that wind through the vineyards from village to village. Here are our favourites, with a word of advice that applies to all of them: the driver tastes and spits, or the driver gets an e-bike day.

France's drink-drive limit is 0.5 g of alcohol per litre of blood, and lower (0.2 g/l) for new drivers. That's less than you might think. Designate a driver, use the spittoon, or plan tastings on e-bike or rest days. Verify the current limits before you travel.

The Alsace wine route runs for about 170 km along the foothills of the Vosges, from Marlenheim near Strasbourg to Thann in the south. It's one of the oldest and best-signposted wine routes in France, and almost certainly the prettiest.

The villages are the stars: Riquewihr, Ribeauvillé, Kaysersberg, Eguisheim, all half-timbered houses, cobbled lanes and window boxes. Alsace wines are named by grape, which makes them easy to learn: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat, Sylvaner, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Noir, plus the sparkling Crémant d'Alsace. Many family winegrowers welcome visitors without appointment.

Burgundy's Route des Grands Crus runs some 60 km from Dijon to Santenay, along the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune. The village names read like a fine wine list: Gevrey-Chambertin, Vougeot, Nuits-Saint-Georges, Pommard, Volnay, Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet.
The landscape is modest (a gentle east-facing slope, stone walls, small villages), but each vineyard plot, or climat, has its own character. The climats of Burgundy are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Base yourself in Beaune and you can explore by car and by bike. The Voie des Vignes cycle path heads south from Beaune through the vineyards, perfect for an e-bike day with a tasting at the end.

Champagne's tourist route is a network of signposted circuits through the main vineyard areas: the Montagne de Reims, the Vallée de la Marne, the Côte des Blancs and the Côte des Bar further south. It's a short hop from Paris, which makes it perfect for a long weekend.

Visit a famous house in Reims or Épernay to see the chalk cellars, then head into the villages to meet growers who make Champagne from their own grapes. Don't miss Hautvillers, where the monk Dom Pérignon worked, or the vineyard lighthouse at Verzenay.

Bordeaux is less a wine route than a wine universe. North of the city, the D2 runs through the Médoc's Route des Châteaux, past the grand estates of Margaux, Saint-Julien, Pauillac and Saint-Estèphe. Many of the most famous châteaux visit by appointment only, so plan ahead.

East of Bordeaux, Saint-Émilion is a medieval village built over its own limestone quarries, with a monolithic church carved into the rock and vineyards all around. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site and arguably the most charming wine village in France. Combine it with the Dordogne for the perfect food-and-wine loop.

The Loire is France's longest river, and its vineyards stretch for hundreds of kilometres, from Sancerre in the east to Muscadet near the Atlantic. In between come Vouvray's Chenin Blanc, the Cabernet Franc reds of Chinon and Bourgueil, and Saumur's sparkling wines.

Many cellars are carved into the soft tufa stone, a cool 12°C all year round, which makes a tasting in July feel even better. And because the landscape is gentle, the Loire is ideal for combining vineyards and châteaux by e-bike.

The northern Rhône's vineyards cling to steep terraces above the river: Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu, Hermitage. Further south, around Avignon and Orange, the landscape opens up into the sun-baked vineyards of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas and Vacqueyras, beneath the jagged Dentelles de Montmirail.
The southern Rhône fits neatly into a Provence road trip: add a day of tastings between the Luberon and Mont Ventoux, and a picnic of local cheese and figs among the vines.
Off the beaten track: Languedoc, Jura and beyond

Some of France's most exciting wine is made away from the famous names. In Languedoc, a new generation of winemakers has transformed regions like Pic Saint-Loup, Faugères and the Minervois, and the landscape of garrigue, Cathar castles and Mediterranean light is a joy to drive. The Jura, between Burgundy and Switzerland, makes nutty vin jaune and straw wines found nowhere else. And Corsica's island grapes, from Nielluccio to Vermentinu, deserve a much wider audience.

These regions tend to be less visited, which means warmer welcomes, lower prices and winemakers who still have time to talk. If you've already done the classics, ask us about building a loop around one of them.
How to plan a wine road trip

Choose a base, not a route. Wine regions are compact, and staying three or four nights in one place means you can taste without moving hotels every day. Mix tasting days with non-wine days (a château, a market, a walk) to keep your palate fresh. And think about the season: late spring brings green vines and quiet cellars; September and October bring the harvest, golden light and a buzz in every village.
Book ahead, especially for smaller estates and anything in Burgundy or Bordeaux. Your specialist can do this for you.
Avoid harvest time for in-depth visits: many winemakers are busy in the vineyards from late August to October. Harvest is still a wonderful time to visit the regions.
Lunch is sacred. Many estates close from noon to two.
Buying a bottle or two after a free tasting at a small estate is appreciated, though rarely expected.
Ask about shipping if you want to buy more than your suitcase can handle.
Every Rond-Point wine loop includes hand-picked tastings with family producers, booked for you, plus plenty of time for the ones you discover yourself.
Alsace, Burgundy, Champagne, Bordeaux, the Loire and the Rhône: France's great wine routes and how to drive them.
Lavender, hill villages and a very long lunch.
Hill villages stacked like sugar cubes, lavender in purple stripes and markets that smell of melon and thyme. Provence is the original slow road trip.

Provence rewards the driver who doesn't hurry. Between the Luberon, the Alpilles and the plateau of Valensole, the roads wriggle past vineyards and olive groves to villages that seem to have been placed on their hilltops for the view: Gordes, Roussillon, Bonnieux, Ménerbes, each with a café terrace and a fountain doing its best.

Head east and the landscape gets dramatic. The Gorges du Verdon cut a 700-metre-deep canyon through the limestone, with rim roads that will test your passengers' nerves and reward them with some of the best views in Europe. To the north, Mont Ventoux looms over everything, white-topped even in summer with bare limestone.
Down on the coast, Cassis and the calanques bring turquoise coves and a fishing-port lunch. The Route des Crêtes above them is short, steep and spectacular.
Our Provence loops are built around markets (every village has a day), long lunches and that early-evening hour when the stone turns gold and the swifts come out.
May–June and September are ideal. Lavender peaks from late June to mid-July; August is hot and busy.
Route des Crêtes, Gorges du Verdon (D23)
A one-way loop from La Palud along the north rim, with belvederes over a 700 m drop. Partly closed in winter.
The famous climb to 1,910 m through forest and then a lunar summit. Usually snow-closed near the top from mid-November to April.
Route des Crêtes, Cassis to La Ciotat (D141)
Some of France's highest sea cliffs, with the calanques far below.
Rosé, olives and a market for every day

Provençal food is sun-driven: tomatoes that taste of something, courgette flowers, tapenade, aïoli on Fridays and lamb from the hills. Every village has a market day, and building your loop around them is half the fun.
The wines run from pale Côtes de Provence rosé to the serious reds of Bandol and the Rhône villages to the north. Lunch at a vineyard with a carafe on the table is not a cliché here; it's a weekday.
Corniches, perched villages and a sea that matches the name.
Three corniche roads stacked above the bluest water in France, and behind them, hill villages and mountain passes most visitors never see.

The Riviera is a driving coast. Between Nice and Menton, the Basse, Moyenne and Grande Corniches run one above the other, each with a different view of the Mediterranean and a different idea of how many hairpins a road needs.

West of Nice, the red rock Corniche de l'Estérel drops into coves between Saint-Raphaël and Cannes, and further on the Corniche des Maures links the beaches of the Var. Inland, Grasse smells of perfume, Saint-Paul-de-Vence of oil paint, and Èze and Gourdon cling to their cliffs.
Go further back and you're in the Alps within an hour: the Col de Turini, the gorges of the Cians and the Var, villages where the bakery doubles as the post office.
May–June and September–October are warm and easier on the roads. February brings mimosa and Menton's lemon festival.
The highest of the three corniches, via La Turbie, with views down on Monaco.
Red porphyry cliffs and coves between Saint-Raphaël and Mandelieu.
Beach after beach between Le Lavandou and Cavalaire, with the Maures hills behind.

Niçois cooking is its own thing: socca (a chickpea pancake) eaten hot from the street, pissaladière with onions and anchovies, stuffed vegetables and the real salade niçoise, which locals will tell you has no cooked vegetables in it.
Look for the tiny Bellet appellation in the hills above Nice, and the rosés of the Var. In Menton, everything comes with lemon.
Castles, caves and a river made for lazy afternoons.
A golden-stone valley with a castle on every cliff, painted caves 20,000 years old and markets where walnuts, foie gras and truffles are taken very seriously.

The Dordogne valley is one of France's great road-trip landscapes. Between Sarlat and the river, the D-roads wind past Beynac, Castelnaud, La Roque-Gageac and Domme, villages so photogenic that you'll stop the car every few kilometres.
The Vézère valley next door is the cradle of prehistoric art, with painted caves and rock shelters around Montignac and Les Eyzies. Book ahead in summer; we'll do it for you.
Further afield, Rocamadour clings to its cliff above the Alzou canyon, and Périgord Vert to the north is all green meadows and Brantôme's abbey on the river.
It's gentle driving and short distances, which leaves plenty of time for a canoe, a picnic and a long dinner on a terrace above the water.
May–June and September–October are perfect. July–August are lively and busy; truffle markets run in winter.
Beynac to La Roque-Gageac and on towards Domme, with castles on both banks.
Montignac to Les Eyzies past cliffs riddled with prehistoric shelters.
The approach from L'Hospitalet gives the classic view of the cliff-hung town.
Truffles, walnuts and the good fat

Périgord cooking is rich and proud of it: duck in every form, potatoes fried in duck fat (pommes sarladaises), walnut cake and, in winter, the black Périgord truffle sold at markets in Sarlat and Sainte-Alvère.
Bergerac and Monbazillac make the local wines, from fresh reds to sweet whites that go astonishingly well with foie gras. Saint-Émilion is under two hours away.
A château for every day of the week.
The garden of France: a broad, lazy river lined with Renaissance châteaux, vineyards and flat, quiet lanes that are made for e-bikes.

The Loire is the gentlest road trip in France. Distances are short, the roads are flat and the châteaux come thick and fast: Chambord, Chenonceau, Amboise, Villandry, Azay-le-Rideau, Chinon, each one different.
It's also the perfect place to leave the car for a day. The Loire à Vélo cycle route follows the river for hundreds of kilometres, with signposted links to the châteaux and plenty of riverside cafés.
West of Tours, the soft tufa stone was quarried for the châteaux, leaving cliffs full of troglodyte homes, mushroom caves and wine cellars around Saumur and Chinon.
April–June for gardens in bloom, September for the harvest. Summer is warm and busy at the big châteaux.
Blois to Tours via Amboise, following the levée with the river alongside.
The troglodyte road, with houses and cellars carved into the cliff.
Loire food is understated and very good: river fish with beurre blanc, rillettes from Tours, goat's cheeses (Sainte-Maure, Selles-sur-Cher, Valençay) and tarte Tatin, born in Sologne.

The wines follow the river: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé upstream, Vouvray's Chenin Blanc around Tours, Chinon and Bourgueil's Cabernet Franc and Saumur's sparkling crémant. Tastings often happen in cellars cut into the rock.
Beaches with stories, cider with bubbles.
Harbour towns that painters adored, the D-Day beaches, orchards full of cider apples and, at the end of the road, an abbey rising out of the sea.

Normandy packs a lot into a short drive. Honfleur's old harbour has inspired painters for 150 years, the Côte Fleurie has belle-époque resorts and long sandy beaches, and inland, the Pays d'Auge is half-timbered farmhouses, orchards and cheese.
Further west, the D-Day landing beaches stretch from Ouistreham to Utah Beach. Museums, cemeteries and memorials tell the story of June 1944, and a good local guide makes it unforgettable.
At the border with Brittany, Mont-Saint-Michel rises from the bay. See it from afar at sunrise, walk across the sands with a guide, and stay nearby so you can visit when the day-trippers have gone.
May–June for apple blossom and long days (and D-Day commemorations around 6 June), September for quieter beaches.
From Ouistreham towards Grandcamp-Maisy, linking Sword, Juno, Gold and Omaha.
A signposted loop through Cambremer and Beuvron-en-Auge with producers along the way.
Honfleur to Trouville above the estuary and the sea.
Butter, cream and four kinds of apple
Normandy cooking runs on butter, cream and apples. Try Camembert, Livarot and Pont-l'Évêque near where they're made, moules à la crème in a harbour town and the salt-marsh lamb of the bay.
Drinks come from the orchard: cider, poiré (perry), Pommeau and Calvados, the apple brandy that locals take mid-meal as a 'trou normand'.
A wild, wind-scrubbed coast of pink granite, lighthouses and secret coves, with crêperies in every village and its own language on the signposts.

Brittany feels like a country of its own, and in some ways it is. Road signs are bilingual, the music is Celtic and the coast seems to go on forever: some 2,700 km of it, with headlands, islands and harbours round every corner.

In the north, Saint-Malo's walled city faces the sea, Cancale is oyster heaven and the Pink Granite Coast near Perros-Guirec is pure geology-as-art. In Finistère, the land ends at the Crozon peninsula and the Pointe du Raz.
The south coast is gentler: Pont-Aven's painters, Concarneau's walled town, the standing stones of Carnac and the island-studded Gulf of Morbihan.
June–September for warm(ish) seas and festivals. Spring and autumn are quieter, with dramatic weather.
Perros-Guirec to Trébeurden along the Pink Granite Coast.
Road to the Pointe du Raz (D784)
From Quimper through Audierne to the westernmost tip of mainland France.
A rugged west-facing coast road on the Quiberon peninsula. Look, don't swim.
Salted butter is a food group
Breton cooking is about the sea and salted butter: oysters from Cancale, scallops, lobster, buckwheat galettes for dinner and sweet crêpes for pudding, kouign-amann for anyone who missed breakfast.
Brittany isn't wine country, so drink cider (brut or doux), served in a bowl, or a local beer. Muscadet from just over the border goes beautifully with the shellfish.
A narrow strip of hillside with the most famous village names in wine, walled vineyards, glazed roofs and an e-bike path that runs right through the middle.

The Côte d'Or is a 60 km ribbon of vines from Dijon to Santenay, and the Route des Grands Crus follows it through Gevrey-Chambertin, Vougeot, Nuits-Saint-Georges, Pommard, Volnay and Meursault. It's a slow road in the best way.

Beaune, with its multicoloured glazed roofs, is the natural base. From there, the Voie des Vignes cycle path heads south through the vineyards, and the Hautes-Côtes behind the escarpment offer quiet lanes and wide views.
Further afield there are Romanesque abbeys, canals for barge-spotting and the Côte Chalonnaise, a less famous and very friendly wine area.
May–June and September–October; harvest is usually in September. Some estates close for visits during harvest.
Route des Grands Crus (D974 and village lanes)
Dijon to Santenay along the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune.
The quiet plateau behind the escarpment, with blackcurrant fields and hilltop views.
Pinot, Chardonnay and something in a cream sauce
Burgundy gave the world boeuf bourguignon, coq au vin and œufs en meurette, plus Dijon mustard, gougères and the pungent Époisses cheese. Lunch is a serious business.

The wines are all about place: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from a patchwork of 'climats', each with its own character. Tasting in a small family cellar is the best way to understand them, and the most fun.
Chalk, cellars and quite a lot of bubbles.
An hour from Paris, rolling vineyards, villages full of small growers and kilometres of chalk cellars beneath Reims and Épernay.

Champagne is a short hop that feels like a proper escape. Reims has a great Gothic cathedral and grand cellars, and Épernay's Avenue de Champagne is lined with famous names. The real charm is in the villages between them.
The Route Touristique du Champagne loops through the Montagne de Reims, the Vallée de la Marne and the Côte des Blancs, with signposted circuits and growers who welcome visitors.
Hautvillers, where the monk Dom Pérignon worked, is a must. So is an e-bike day through the vines: the hills are short, the views are long and the tastings are close together.
May–June for green vines, September for the harvest, December for festive cellars. Very quiet in January–February.
Route Touristique du Champagne, Montagne de Reims
Reims to Épernay via Verzenay, its lighthouse among the vines, and Hautvillers.
Chardonnay country, from Cramant and Avize to Le Mesnil-sur-Oger and Vertus.
Biscuits roses and a glass of something
Champagne's food is hearty and northern: jambon de Reims, Chaource cheese, potée champenoise and the pink Reims biscuits locals dunk in their glass.

Beyond the big houses, more than 4,000 growers make their own Champagne. Visiting a récoltant-manipulant (grower who makes and sells their own) is one of the joys of the region, and very different from a big cellar tour.
A wine road threaded through storybook villages between the Vosges and the Rhine, with Germanic food, French flair and the best Christmas markets in the country.

The Route des Vins d'Alsace runs some 170 km along the foothills of the Vosges, and it's one of the most rewarding drives in France. Riquewihr, Ribeauvillé, Kaysersberg, Eguisheim and Obernai look almost too pretty, with half-timbered houses and window boxes spilling geraniums.

Above them, ruined castles crown the hills and the restored Haut-Kœnigsbourg watches over the plain. Higher still, the Route des Crêtes follows the Vosges ridges with views to the Black Forest and, on clear days, the Alps.
Colmar and Strasbourg make fine bookends: canals, museums and some of the most atmospheric old towns in Europe.
May–June and September–October for the wine road, late November to Christmas Eve for the markets.
Marlenheim to Thann, through more than 60 wine villages.
Along the ridges from the Col du Bonhomme to the Grand Ballon. Upper sections close in winter.
Tarte flambée and seven grape varieties
Alsace cooking is generous: choucroute garnie, baeckeoffe, tarte flambée (flammekueche) from wood-fired ovens, Munster cheese and kugelhopf for breakfast. A winstub is the place to eat it.
Alsace wines are named by grape: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat, Sylvaner, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Noir, plus 51 Grand Cru vineyards and excellent Crémant d'Alsace.
Surf, red shutters and the Pyrenees as a backdrop.
Atlantic surf towns, green hills, red-and-white villages and a culture all its own, where the Pyrenees meet the sea.

The Pays Basque packs mountains and ocean into a small corner. Biarritz has belle-époque glamour and serious surf, Saint-Jean-de-Luz a perfect harbour and a sheltered beach, and the Corniche Basque runs along cliff tops towards Spain.
Inland, the hills roll up to the Pyrenees: Espelette with its strings of red peppers, Ainhoa and Sare among the most beautiful villages in France, and La Rhune, the mountain with the rack railway.
Further in, Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port welcomes pilgrims heading for Santiago, the Irouléguy vineyards climb steep terraces and the Iraty forest is one of the largest beech forests in Europe.
May–June and September–October for warm days and fewer crowds; summer brings fêtes, and autumn the biggest swells.
Cliff-top road from Socoa to Hendaye.
Through green valleys and red-shuttered villages into the Pyrenean foothills.
High mountain roads through beech forest and pasture. Some sections close in winter.

Basque food is a celebration: Bayonne ham, axoa (veal with Espelette pepper), sheep's cheese with black cherry jam, chipirons (baby squid) and gâteau basque, filled with cream or cherries depending on who you ask.
Drink Irouléguy reds and rosés from the mountain terraces, Basque cider in season and Jurançon's sweet whites from neighbouring Béarn.
Grand cru country and Europe's tallest sand dune.
A handsome city on the Garonne, the world's most famous vineyards on its doorstep and an Atlantic coast of endless beaches and pine forest.
Bordeaux is a gateway city: elegant 18th-century streets, a huge riverside promenade and a food scene that's grown up fast. From there, the vineyards fan out in every direction.

North, the Médoc's Route des Châteaux runs past the great names of Margaux and Pauillac. East, Saint-Émilion is a medieval village perched over its own limestone quarries, surrounded by vines. South, Sauternes makes golden sweet wines.
West, the Atlantic: the Bassin d'Arcachon's oyster villages, the Dune du Pilat and long straight roads through the Landes pine forest to surf beaches that seem to go on for ever.
May–June and September–October; the vendanges usually run through September into October.
From the edge of Bordeaux through Margaux, Pauillac and Saint-Estèphe.
Narrow lanes around the village through some of the most famous Merlot in the world.
Oysters, entrecôte and a very long wine list

Bordeaux eats well: Arcachon oysters with a glass of Entre-Deux-Mers, entrecôte à la bordelaise grilled over vine cuttings, lamprey for the brave, and canelés, the little caramelised cakes that are everywhere.

The wines need no introduction, but they reward exploring beyond the famous labels: Côtes de Bourg, Entre-Deux-Mers, Graves and the satellite appellations around Saint-Émilion offer great value and warm welcomes.
Cathar castles, wild gorges and big-hearted wine.
France's sunniest secret: medieval Carcassonne, Cathar castles on impossible crags, deep river gorges and some of the best-value wine in the country.

Languedoc is Provence's wilder sibling. Carcassonne's double ring of walls is the headline, but the real adventure is in the hills to the south, where the Cathar castles of Peyrepertuse and Quéribus balance on the ridges.
North, the Hérault and the Tarn have carved deep gorges. Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert is a medieval village tucked into a canyon, and the Gorges du Tarn are a classic drive.
Along the coast, the Canal du Midi reaches the sea, oysters come from the Étang de Thau and Montpellier makes a lively, young base.
Spring and autumn are glorious; July–August are hot, and the coast gets busy.
Carcassonne into the Corbières hills to Peyrepertuse and Quéribus.
From Ispagnac to Le Rozier between limestone walls and the river.
From the Pont du Diable to Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert and beyond.
Languedoc food is southern and generous: cassoulet in Castelnaudary and Carcassonne, Bouzigues oysters, tielle (octopus pie) from Sète and Roquefort from the caves next door.

Once known for quantity, Languedoc wine is now one of France's most exciting regions: Pic Saint-Loup, Faugères, Minervois and Corbières reds, plus sparkling Blanquette de Limoux, which locals will tell you is older than Champagne.
Above the clouds, two hands on the wheel.
The highest paved passes in Europe, glacier views, lakes like mirrors and the Route des Grandes Alpes from Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean.

For anyone who loves driving, the Alps are the promised land. The Route des Grandes Alpes crosses more than 15 passes on its way from Thonon-les-Bains to Menton, and almost every one of them is a legend: the Iseran, the Galibier, the Izoard, the Bonette.
Between the passes are lakes (Annecy, Serre-Ponçon), old fortified towns like Briançon, and quiet valleys such as the Ubaye and the Queyras, where marmots whistle at passing cars.
The high passes are generally open from around June to October, depending on snow. Outside those months, the Alps become ski country, and we'll happily build you a winter loop instead.
Late June to September for the high passes (opening dates vary with snow). December–March for snow.
Lanslebourg to Val d'Isère via Bonneval-sur-Arc over 2,764 m, the highest paved pass in the Alps. Usually open June–October.
Valloire to the Col du Lautaret over 2,642 m, a Tour de France favourite.
Lake Geneva to Menton across the great passes. Our riviera loop borrows its southern half.
Alpine food is built for altitude: tartiflette, fondue, raclette, crozets and the great cheeses (Beaufort, Reblochon, Abondance, Tomme de Savoie) made in high summer pastures.
Savoie wines are fresh and mountainous: Apremont and Chignin whites, spicy Mondeuse reds, and génépi, the herbal liqueur that appears after dinner whether you asked for it or not.
A mountain in the sea, and every road knows it.
Red granite cliffs, turquoise coves, chestnut forests and mountain villages. Corsica is France's wildest road trip, with bends to match.

The 'Île de Beauté' is a mountain range rising out of the Mediterranean, and driving it is an adventure. Roads are narrow and winding, distances take twice as long as the map suggests, and the views are worth every hairpin.

On the west coast, the Calanches de Piana are a jumble of red rock above the Gulf of Porto, with the Scandola nature reserve beyond. In the north, the Balagne's hill villages look over the sea, and Cap Corse points at mainland Italy.

The interior is wild: Corte and the Restonica gorge, the forests of Vizzavona, the Aiguilles de Bavella. In the south, Bonifacio sits on white cliffs facing Sardinia, and the beaches around Porto-Vecchio are as good as anywhere in the Mediterranean.
May–June and September–October are perfect. July–August are hot and busy, with ferries full.
Piana to Porto through red granite spires. Narrow: expect to reverse for a coach at least once.
Solenzara to Zonza beneath the jagged Aiguilles de Bavella.
A loop round the island's northern finger, past Genoese towers and fishing ports.

Corsican food comes from the maquis and the mountains: charcuterie from free-roaming pigs (figatellu, coppa, lonzu), brocciu ewe's-milk cheese, chestnut flour in everything from cakes to beer, and wild boar stew.
The island's wines are distinctive, with local grapes like Nielluccio and Sciaccarellu (reds) and Vermentinu (whites). Patrimonio, Ajaccio and Calvi are good names to look for.

Purple fields, villages balanced on hilltops and a market for every morning: Provence's greatest hits, linked by the back roads.

This loop starts and ends at Marseille and takes in the three Provences: the Luberon's hill villages, the lavender plateaux of Sault and Valensole, and the calanques coast at Cassis. Driving days are a comfortable two hours or so, with every afternoon left free for wandering.

Time it for late June or July and the lavender is in full, ridiculous bloom. Come in May or September and you'll have the villages almost to yourself, with markets in full swing and the sea still warm.
Gordes, Roussillon and Bonnieux, the Luberon's most beautiful hill villages

Pick up the car and head north to Lourmarin for a first coffee on a plane-tree square. By teatime you're by a pool among the olive trees.
Shop the market with a local cook and turn it into lunch. Afternoon: four villages, one ochre cliff and more photos than strictly necessary.
Ventoux and the lavender of Sault
Past the abbey's lavender to the plateau of Sault, then up the Giant of Provence. The summit looks like the moon, if the moon sold nougat.
Through Forcalquier to the plateau of Valensole, where the lavender runs to the horizon in tidy purple stripes. Visit a family distillery to see where it all ends up.
Paddle into the mouth of the Verdon gorges on water the colour of mouthwash, then climb to Moustiers' star, strung between two cliffs since the Middle Ages.
Lunch under the plane trees of Aix's Cours Mirabeau, then down to Cassis in time for a swim and a harbourside apéritif.
The Route des Crêtes in the morning, a hill village and a Bandol tasting at lunch. Back in Cassis, a boat to the calanques if you've still got energy.
A last croissant by the harbour and an easy drive to the airport. The loop is closed; the lavender stays in your suitcase.
Gorges du Verdon & the Route Napoléon
Loop from Nice Côte d'Azur Airport
The emperor's road, Europe's grandest canyon and three Alpine passes, with the Riviera as a finish line. For people who think the drive is the destination.

Napoleon marched north from the coast in 1815 along the road that now bears his name. You'll follow him up through Grasse and Castellane, then turn off for the Gorges du Verdon, where rim roads hang above a 700-metre drop.

From there it's up into the Alps of Haute-Provence: the Ubaye valley, the Col de la Cayolle and the red gorges of Daluis, before you drop back to the sea and finish with the Riviera's corniches and the rally roads of the Col de Turini. Ambitious, yes. Unforgettable, definitely.
The Route Napoléon from Grasse to Castellane

Leave the coast through the Gorges du Loup, blend a perfume in Grasse, then join the Route Napoléon for the climb to Castellane. Unlike the emperor, you'll have air conditioning.
The Route des Crêtes loops along the north rim with a belvedere at every bend. Seventy-five kilometres has never taken so long, or been so worth it.
The south rim's Corniche Sublime, then back along the canyon for a late swim in the lake. Paddle in if the arms still work.
Across the Valensole plateau (purple in early summer), through Digne and up into the Ubaye valley, where the air thins and the cheese thickens.
Over the 2,326 m Cayolle on a road barely wider than the car, then through the wine-red gorges of Daluis to Vauban's fortress at Entrevaux. Sea by sunset.
Lemons in Menton, then the hairpins of the Col de Turini, famous from the Monte Carlo Rally. Drive it like a tourist, not a rally driver.
The long way to the airport
One last loop along the Grande Corniche via Èze and La Turbie before you hand back the keys, a little reluctantly.

Seven days, a dozen châteaux and three days on two wheels. The flattest, friendliest road trip in France.

From Tours, an hour from Paris by TGV, this loop links the greatest Renaissance châteaux with short, easy drives. You'll base yourself first near Amboise, then in medieval Chinon, so you're never packing and unpacking.

Three days are on e-bikes, on the Loire à Vélo route and quiet vineyard lanes: Chenonceau by bike, Chinon's wine villages and Saumur's troglodyte cliffs. Pedal-assist makes it easy; the tastings make it memorable.
Chenonceau by e-bike, arriving the way the gardeners do
Chambord's double-helix staircase and Blois' royal château

Collect the car in Tours and follow the river to Amboise, with a Vouvray tasting on the way. Château-spotting starts immediately.
The car has a day off. Pedal through forest and vines to Chenonceau, the château that bridges the Cher, with a picnic on the way back.
Quiet lanes and forest tracks; one gentle climb out of the valley.
Chambord's 400-odd rooms and Leonardo-inspired staircase, then the royal château of Blois. Dinner back in Amboise, under the château walls.
The vegetable gardens of Villandry, laid out like embroidery, and Azay-le-Rideau, floating on its moat. Chinon by aperitif time.
Ride the riverbank to where the Vienne meets the Loire, then taste Chinon reds in a cellar cut deep into the rock.
Mostly flat riverside paths, with one short climb to the vineyards.
Drive to Saumur via Fontevraud Abbey, then switch to e-bikes for the troglodyte road, where people still live in the cliff.
Cliff-foot lanes and a loop through the vineyards above Saumur.
An easy hour back to Tours and the TGV. You'll be in Paris before your goat's cheese has warmed up.
Château tickets for Chenonceau, Chambord and Villandry
The world's most famous wine road, explored by car and by e-bike, with Beaune as your base and a cellar at the end of every lane.

From Dijon, the Route des Grands Crus runs south through a roll-call of legendary villages: Gevrey-Chambertin, Vougeot, Nuits-Saint-Georges. You'll stay five nights in Beaune, so the car can rest as often as you do.

Three e-bike days follow the Voie des Vignes and quiet lanes through Pommard, Meursault, the Côte de Nuits and the Côte Chalonnaise. The rides are short, the hills are gentle, and the tastings are, frankly, the point.
