Collect the car and drive the most expensive 45 km of vines on earth. Try not to scratch anything.
Pedal the Voie des Vignes from your door, with lunch in Meursault and a tasting on the way home.
A dedicated cycle path through the vines, plus a few short village climbs.
Up behind the escarpment to the Hautes-Côtes and the fortified village of Châteauneuf, then back for an evening tasting with a family winemaker.
A short drive south to the friendly Côte Chalonnaise for an e-bike loop on the Voie Verte. Less famous, less expensive, equally delicious.
A former railway line turned greenway, nearly flat.
Côte de Nuits on two wheels
Drive to Nuits, then ride the lanes past the walled Clos de Vougeot to Chambolle-Musigny. Grand cru names on every signpost.
Vineyard lanes with short, punchy climbs between villages.
Back to Dijon in time for its covered market. Buy mustard. Buy more mustard than seems wise.
Guided e-bike day with vineyard tasting
Storybook villages, castles on the hills and seven grape varieties to get to know. Alsace is the gentlest kind of road trip, and the prettiest.

From Strasbourg, the Route des Vins d'Alsace leads south through village after half-timbered village. You'll stay five nights in one wine village, with short drives each day and plenty of time to linger.
Add a day on the Route des Crêtes along the Vosges ridges, a castle or two and an evening in Colmar's Petite Venise. Come in December and it all comes wrapped in fairy lights.
A tasting across the Alsace grapes with a family winegrower
The Haut-Kœnigsbourg castle above the vineyards
The Route des Crêtes along the Vosges ridges
Colmar's Petite Venise and its canals
Tarte flambée in a proper winstub
Leave Strasbourg on the Route des Vins, stopping in Obernai's market square. Every village looks like a cake decoration, and that's before the cake.
Morning at the Haut-Kœnigsbourg, afternoon tasting your way from Riesling to Gewurztraminer. Storks optional but likely.
Two of the prettiest villages in France and a night watchman's town in between. Eguisheim is built in circles, which we take as a sign.
Up into the Vosges for a ridge road with views to the Black Forest. Lunch at a mountain farm-inn: Munster, potatoes, no regrets.
A slow day in Colmar's canals and covered market, with time for the Unterlinden museum. Back for a last winstub dinner.
Return to Strasbourg with the afternoon free for the cathedral and Petite France. The boot will clink; that's normal.
A castle on every cliff, art 20,000 years old and a river to float down. Finish among the vines of Saint-Émilion.

From Bordeaux, you'll head east through Saint-Émilion's vineyards to the Périgord Noir, where the Dordogne winds beneath Beynac, Castelnaud and La Roque-Gageac. Five nights in one golden-stone manor mean plenty of time for canoes, caves and markets.

Day trips take in the prehistoric caves of the Vézère, cliff-hung Rocamadour and a truffle farm. Then it's back west via Périgueux and Brantôme to finish with two nights among the Saint-Émilion vines.
Canoeing beneath the castles of Beynac and Castelnaud
Prehistoric cave art in the Vézère valley
Sarlat's Saturday market and a truffle hunt
Two nights among the vines of Saint-Émilion
Lunch in Bergerac, then along the river into the Périgord Noir. Your first castle appears before the first coffee wears off.
Canoe past three castles, then drive up to the bastide of Domme for the view back down the valley you've just paddled.
Bison, horses and aurochs painted 20,000 years ago, plus a cliff village that housed people from prehistory to the Middle Ages.
A pilgrims' town stacked up a cliff, and a boat ride on an underground river 100 metres down. Opposites attract.
Sarlat's market first, then follow a truffle dog through the oaks. Afternoon at Hautefort, the Périgord's grandest château.
Through Périgueux to Brantôme, its abbey reflected in the river, then south-west to the vines of Saint-Émilion for two nights.
A morning tasting at a family château, then a loop through the Entre-Deux-Mers bastide towns. Evening: the monolithic church, by the light of a glass.
Back to Bordeaux with a boot full of walnut oil and good intentions about using it.
Loop from Paris (Charles de Gaulle Airport or city centre)
Monet's garden, Honfleur's harbour, the beaches of June 1944 and the abbey in the bay, with plenty of cider in between.

From Paris, the loop heads west via Monet's garden at Giverny to Honfleur, then through the half-timbered Pays d'Auge to Bayeux. A full day with a local historian on the D-Day beaches is the emotional heart of the trip.
Then on to Mont-Saint-Michel, where you'll stay by the bay, walk across the sands with a guide and see the abbey when the crowds have gone. The return takes the long way back via Honfleur.
Monet's house and gardens at Giverny
Honfleur's old harbour and the Côte Fleurie

Monet's garden in the morning, Honfleur's harbour by evening. The light really is that good; the painters weren't exaggerating.
Through orchards and half-timbered villages, tasting cider, Pommeau and a sensible amount of Calvados (the driver gets the Camembert).
A local historian joins you for the day, from the Mulberry harbour at Arromanches to the cliffs of Pointe du Hoc. Moving, and never rushed.
The tapestry in the morning, copper-pan town Villedieu at lunch, and the first sight of the Mont rising out of the bay.
Walk barefoot across the bay with a qualified guide, timed to the tides, then explore the abbey once the day-trippers have left.
East again, with a seafood lunch at Trouville's fish market and the evening on Honfleur's quays.
A straight run back to Paris, with a cooler bag of butter and cheese that the airline will have opinions about.
Full-day D-Day beaches tour with a local historian
Walled cities, pink granite, the end of the world and an inland sea full of islands. A full lap of Brittany's coast, one crêperie at a time.

From Rennes, the loop runs clockwise around Brittany's coast: Saint-Malo and Cancale, the Pink Granite Coast, the wild peninsulas of Finistère and the gentler south, from Concarneau to the Gulf of Morbihan.
It's a balanced pace with four bases, so you're never on the road too long. Expect coastal walks, oysters, lighthouses and weather that changes every twenty minutes, which is all part of the charm.
Saint-Malo's ramparts and oysters at Cancale
The rocks of Ploumanac'h on the Pink Granite Coast
The Crozon peninsula and the Pointe du Raz
Concarneau's walled Ville Close and Pont-Aven
A sailing trip on the Gulf of Morbihan
Via medieval Dinan to Saint-Malo, in time to walk the ramparts at sunset. Low tide reveals the island tombs; high tide hides them again.
Out to the oyster beds at Cancale with a producer, then across the Rance to belle-époque Dinard.
The heather-topped cliffs of Cap Fréhel and a castle on a rock, then west to the Pink Granite Coast.
Walk the customs officers' path among boulders shaped like hats, tortoises and, if you squint, your uncle.
To the end of the earth
The big day: across Finistère to the cliffs of the Crozon peninsula, then the granite village of Locronan and south to Concarneau.
The westernmost tip of mainland France, where the Atlantic arrives with feeling. Galettes in Quimper on the way back.
Gauguin's Pont-Aven, 3,000 standing stones at Carnac and the wild west coast of Quiberon, all before dinner.
Sail between the islands with a local skipper, then wander Vannes' half-timbered old town.
One last flower-covered village at Rochefort-en-Terre, then Rennes and the train home, smelling faintly of salted butter.
Half-day sail on the Gulf of Morbihan
Surf in the morning, red-shuttered villages after lunch and an e-bike along cliffs that face Spain. The Basque Country does a bit of everything, beautifully.

This loop from Biarritz splits its time between the coast at Saint-Jean-de-Luz and the green hills around Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port. Three e-bike days cover the Corniche Basque, the pepper village of Espelette and the coast from Bayonne to Biarritz.
In between, you'll drive into the Pyrenean foothills, through the vast Iraty beech forest and among the steep Irouléguy vineyards. Bring an appetite: this is one of France's great food regions.
E-biking the Corniche Basque from Saint-Jean-de-Luz to Hendaye
Espelette, Ainhoa and Sare, three of France's most beautiful villages
A surf lesson on a forgiving Basque beach
The Iraty forest and the Holzarte footbridge
Bayonne's old town and Biarritz's belle-époque seafront
A short hop to Saint-Jean-de-Luz, its harbour and its beach. Afternoon: a surf lesson. Evening: a lot of tapas, earned.
E-bike along the cliff tops to Hendaye with the Pyrenees dropping into the sea. Swim, coffee, swim, ride home.
Cliff-top lanes with rolling climbs; quiet coastal roads and cycle paths.
Drive inland to Espelette, its houses strung with drying red peppers, then e-bike a loop through the hills to Ainhoa.
Hilly but short; the motor does the heavy lifting.
Up the Nive valley to Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, where pilgrims set off for Santiago. You'll set off for a tasting among the Irouléguy terraces.
Iraty and the Pays de Soule
High roads through one of Europe's largest beech forests, wild horses on the pastures and a wobbly footbridge over the Holzarte gorge.
Ham and chocolate in Bayonne, then e-bike the coast path to Biarritz's lighthouse and the Rocher de la Vierge.
Coastal cycle paths through Anglet's pine woods to Biarritz.
A final gâteau basque for the road and twenty minutes to the airport. Agur means goodbye, but nobody says it like they mean it.
Surf lesson with board and wetsuit
Red cliffs, mountain gorges, chestnut forests and beaches that look edited. Ten days to circle France's wildest island, one hairpin at a time.

Corsica is a mountain range in the sea, and this loop shows you both halves. From Ajaccio you'll drive the Calanches de Piana, take a boat to Scandola, wind round the coast to the Balagne and cross the island to Corte.

Then it's south over the Col de Bavella to the Gulf of Valinco for four nights, with day trips to Bonifacio's white cliffs and the villages of the Alta Rocca. The roads are slow and narrow, the distances short and the views constant. Allow time to stop, and to reverse for the odd coach.
The Calanches de Piana, red granite above the Gulf of Porto

North along the coast to Cargèse, then into the red granite of the Calanches. Arrive at Piana in time for sunset over the gulf.
A morning boat from Porto to the Scandola reserve and Girolata, then a walk in the Spelunca gorge among old Genoese bridges.
The wild coastal road to Galéria and Calvi's citadel, then up to a hill village. A long day in the car; you'll want every minute of it.
Artisans' villages perched above the sea, then Saint-Florent and a Patrimonio tasting. Somebody else should do that bit; it's island wine.
Cross to the island's old capital, Corte, and drive up the Restonica gorge for a swim in a granite pool, if you dare the temperature.
The big one: down the east coast, then up over the Col de Bavella beneath its jagged granite needles, and through Sartène to the Gulf of Valinco.
Past the lion-shaped rock at Roccapina to Bonifacio, balanced on white limestone cliffs above a fjord-like harbour.
Carved standing stones at Filitosa, then the long white beach at Campomoro with its Genoese tower. Afternoon off: you've earned it.
Stone villages in the chestnut forests, river pools and a long lunch of charcuterie and brocciu.

From palm trees to glaciers and back: the Riviera corniches, then the greatest passes of the Route des Grandes Alpes. A driver's trip, with views to match.

Start with two days on the Riviera: the corniches above Monaco, the red rocks of the Estérel and lunch by the sea. Then head north through the Gorges du Cians into the high Alps, where every day brings a legendary col.

The Bonette, the Izoard, the Galibier and the Col de l'Iseran, the highest paved pass in the Alps, are all on the menu. The return takes the Col d'Allos and the Var valley back to the sea. The high passes usually open from June to October, so this loop runs in summer only.

Antibes' old town, a quick Croisette swagger in Cannes, then the red-rock Corniche d'Or. Swim in a cove, motorway home.

The road loops round the summit of the Bonette at 2,802 m, one of the highest paved roads in Europe. Bring a jumper; it's August down below, not up here.
Three great cols in one day, the lunar Casse Déserte and lunch in Vauban's fortified Briançon. Legendary stuff.

Down the Maurienne to the stone village of Bonneval, then over the Iseran, 2,764 m and often lined with snow walls in June. Lunch in Val d'Isère, then back the same way, which looks completely different.
Back over the Galibier and south past Embrun to Serre-Ponçon, a turquoise lake perfect for a swim stop.
Over the Col d'Allos and down the Var valley past fortified Colmars and Entrevaux. From snow to sea in an afternoon.
A final coffee in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, then the airport. Your brakes will thank you; your camera won't.

A honey-stone farmhouse below a Luberon village, with a pool among the olive trees and a breakfast table that runs to four kinds of jam. Three exits from the drive, all of them lead somewhere lovely.
La Bastide de la Quatrième Sortie
A small bastide between the lavender of Valensole and the cliffs of Moustiers. Shutters the colour of the plateau in July, and a terrace built for long evenings.
A white villa above the harbour at Cassis, where you can watch the fishing boats come in from the breakfast table. The only wrong way here is leaving early.
A stone inn near Castellane for everyone who missed the motorway exit and found the Route Napoléon instead. Hearty dinners, thick walls and the Verdon on the doorstep.
A pastel villa on the hillside above Villefranche-sur-Mer, with a sea view from every room. Close enough to Nice for dinner, far enough for peace.
A larch-wood chalet in the Ubaye valley at Barcelonnette, surrounded by some of the highest passes in Europe. Big breakfasts for big climbs.
A mountain hotel in Valloire, between the Galibier and the Télégraphe. Named for the question every driver asks on the way up: how many more hairpins?
A turreted château near Amboise with a walled potager, a moat that's mostly decorative and bikes waiting by the door. Fairy tale, with good Wi-Fi.
A townhouse in medieval Chinon with a garden that looks up at the fortress. Cool tufa cellars below, warm welcome above.
A winemaker's house inside the ramparts of Beaune, with vaulted cellars and a courtyard made for apéritifs. The Côte d'Or starts at the end of the street.
La Maison de la Bulle Ronde
A belle-époque house in Épernay, a short stroll from the avenue of famous cellars. Breakfast comes with a view of the vines and, on request, a little fizz.
A half-timbered house around a flowery courtyard in a Route des Vins village. Window boxes, wooden beams and a winstub two doors down.
A golden-stone manor above the Dordogne near Beynac, with a pool facing three castles. You'll want to turn back for one more night. Everyone does.
A small wine château outside Saint-Émilion with rooms above the chai and vines up to the terrace. Dinner is paired, naturally.
A slate-hung townhouse a few steps from Honfleur's old harbour, the last exit before the sea. Painters came for the light; you'll stay for the breakfast butter.
A half-timbered farmhouse outside Bayeux, among apple orchards and very calm cows. The ideal base for the D-Day beaches.
Les Grèves de la Grande Boucle
A stone house on the edge of the bay, with Mont-Saint-Michel framed in the bedroom window. Set an alarm for sunrise; you won't regret it.
A privateer's country manor on the edge of Saint-Malo, with walled gardens and granite fireplaces. Swashbuckling optional.
A Breton 'ty' (house) on the Pink Granite Coast, with a garden that runs down to the coastal path. Fall asleep to the tide, wake up to salted-butter everything.
Whitewashed rooms by the water near Concarneau, with the walled Ville Close across the bay. Fishing boats at dawn, crêpes at dusk.
Le Manoir du Tour du Golfe
A granite manor on the Gulf of Morbihan, the inland sea with an island for every day of the year (give or take). Boats leave from the bottom of the garden.
A red-shuttered Basque house above Saint-Jean-de-Luz. 'Biribil' means round in Euskara, which seemed right. Surfboards and e-bikes in the garage.
A restored shepherd's farmhouse in the hills near Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, among Irouléguy vines and grazing sheep. Itzulia means 'the return'; you'll see why.
A cliff-top hotel at Piana looking over the red granite Calanches and the Gulf of Porto. A thousand bends to get here, one view that makes them all worth it.
A stone house in a Balagne hill village, with a terrace over olive groves and the sea beyond. Two loops of the island on the guestbook, and counting.
A mountain guesthouse near Corte, the island's old capital, at the mouth of the Restonica gorge. Chestnut flour on the breakfast table and silence at night.
Hôtel du Retour au Point de Départ
A beach-side hotel on the Gulf of Valinco, where the loop starts thinking about coming home. Four nights here, so unpack properly.
